title: Are you ignoring this key group in your school policy decisions? https://www.tes.com/magazine/leadership/strategy/how-to-bring-pupils-into-school-policy-decisions
author: Christopher Burn
summary: Christopher Burn, a primary teacher at Malvern College Egypt, argues that schools consult teachers carefully when writing policy but rarely ask the pupils who experience it. He describes how his school, after designing and trialling a research-informed Feedback and Feedforward Policy with a staff working group, surveyed key stage 2 pupils with short anonymous Likert-scale questionnaires delivered from a common script. Because surveys only show where to look, the school followed up with paired interviews in a neutral setting, deliberately choosing pupils across ages, attainment levels, gender and additional needs, including pupils with English as an additional language and pupils with dyslexia. Pupils valued improvement time and teacher shout-outs, but most prized simple clarifying conversations with teachers, and they reported that feedback felt different across subjects. Burn uses these findings to argue for policies that give direction without over-prescription and to help teachers prioritise live and whole-class feedback. He insists that pupil voice is evidence rather than a veto, and closes that policies written in meeting rooms succeed or fail in classrooms.
points: Burn's school paired anonymous pupil surveys with paired interviews, using survey patterns to decide where to probe.
Interviewees were chosen for diversity of age, attainment and need rather than articulacy, to avoid hearing only confident voices.
The most valued feedback turned out to be simple conversations with teachers, which the policy designers had not anticipated.
He frames pupil voice as one strand of evidence alongside research and professional expertise, explicitly not a veto on policy.
quotes: Schools rightly place teachers at the heart of policy development. They understand where the friction points lie, what is manageable in the classroom and how change is likely to be received.
But a survey can only take you so far. The patterns told us where to look; conversations helped us understand why.
The power dynamic matters. Pupils spend much of their school day trying to give teachers the “right” answer, so asking what they really think requires some thought.
Rather than choosing the most articulate, confident pupils, we deliberately sought different voices across ages, classes, attainment, gender and additional needs.
Again and again, they pointed to the value of simple conversations with teachers to clarify, question and deepen their understanding.

Of course, pupil voice isn’t pupil veto. Listening to pupils does not mean handing over policy decisions; their experiences are another valuable source of evidence alongside research, professional expertise and the school’s wider priorities.
After all, while policies are written in meeting rooms, they usually succeed or fail in classrooms.
